intro: Five long reads for a slow week: how AI could end the rule of America's working rich, why mosquito-borne disease is now a regulatory choice, what an always-listening machine does to the self, why the brain's electrical waves may be doing real work, and where export controls can and cannot touch open-weight AI.

stories.headline: The last ruling class that had to work
stories.dek: Branko Milanović and Nils Gilman argue that AI will end the forty-year settlement in which America's richest people also held its best-paid jobs, and that neither ending is good for democracy.
body: In 1941 the American writer James Burnham predicted that capitalism was finished. It would give way, he thought, to 'managerialism': a system in which the state controlled production and handed its running to the people who actually understood it. Socialism was utopian, because it required an abundance nobody could supply; private property, and the ideology that defended it, were on their way out.

Burnham was wrong about the politics: America returned enthusiastically to private property by the 1980s, and communism collapsed. Yet Branko Milanović, an economist of inequality, and Nils Gilman argue in Noema that his central question has never been more pressing: who controls the instruments of production, and what class does that control create?

Their answer is that the managers did rise, but into capital rather than against it. The result is a ruling class with little precedent, sitting at the top of the wage distribution and the wealth distribution at the same time. Artificial intelligence, they contend, is about to break it, one way or the other.
## Rich twice over

Milanović's name for this group is homoploutia, from the Greek for 'same' and 'wealth': people who are rich from their labour and rich from their capital at once. The authors call it the most significant structural change in capitalism since the second world war. In America about 30% of the top income decile qualifies, roughly 3% of the population, and the share has risen steadily since the early 1980s, tracking rising income inequality and falling mobility between generations. Elsewhere it is rarer: under 1% of the population in Mexico, and around 2-2.5% in Spain, Italy, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. America is the extreme case, which is why it is instructive.

The figures on capital income show how narrow the base is. Sixty per cent of American households have zero or negligible capital income; the share is 79% in Spain, 93% in Colombia and 96% in Peru, on 2021 data. In 2022 the top 1% of American capitalists received nearly $100,000 each in capital income, about $400,000 a year for a family of four from interest, dividends, rents and private pensions alone. The wider homoploutic class takes about $20,500 a head, or over $80,000 a family.

The position is strong because it is diversified. A household drawing on both wages and capital is cushioned either way: a bad year for shares is absorbed by salaries, a lost job by the portfolio. The authors suggest this is the one development in capitalism that would have surprised Marx, because it internalises class conflict within a single household.
## The meritocratic alibi

Such a class needs a story, and its story is merit. Wealth is said to reflect talent and effort, and the road is said to remain open to gifted outsiders. The authors lean on the law professor Daniel Markovits, whose 2019 book 'The Meritocracy Trap' called this an ideological conceit that launders an unjust allocation of advantage. By the end of graduate school, on the figure they cite, parental investment in an elite child's education comes to about $10m, an inheritance in all but name.

They rewrite Marx's circuit of capital, M-C-M', in which money buys commodities to make more money, as M-E-M', where E is the education of one's children. If entry to the right schools requires parental wealth, mobility closes while the rhetoric of merit stays wide open.

Nor is this the 1960s technocracy of Galbraith or Tinbergen, which expected East and West to converge on efficient management whoever owned the factories. Here interest and ideology align perfectly: the homoplouts defend capital because they are capital.
## Two ways to end
The essay turns on an empirical question nobody can yet answer: will AI substitute for high-paid cognitive labour, or complement it? The two answers produce opposite futures.

In the first, AI raises capital's share of income, the profit rate holds up as old capital is destroyed and replaced, and homoplouts keep their well-paid jobs while buying stakes in the growing sectors. The class expands from a third of the top labour-income decile to half or two-thirds. Eventually the top 10% by wages and the top 10% by capital become the same people, advantage passes reliably through schooling and inheritance, and today's top 3% of Americans hardens into a self-reproducing aristocracy. Homoploutia turns out to be a way-station back to hereditary hierarchy.

In the second, AI strikes the homoplouts where they earn. Their wage premiums come from being lawyers, financiers, consultants, software engineers and doctors, the sophisticated cognitive work that, as the roboticist Hans Moravec observed, is easier to automate than the sensorimotor skills evolution spent a billion years building. If machines substitute for that work, the salary leg of the household gives way. The rich revert to classical rentiers who no longer work, and America begins to resemble Mexico, where the rich mostly do not.

Either way, the authors argue, meritocracy loses its alibi. If the class entrenches, entry comes only by inheritance and claims of merit ring hollow. If it dissolves, education no longer commands a premium, so work no longer signals merit; one simply owns things. The roughly forty-year settlement in which the same people held the best jobs and the most property, and pointed to the first to justify the second, is ending one way or another.
## A pyramid with no middle

What replaces it looks pre-industrial. At the summit sit a few thousand people who own the models. Below them is a closed homoploutic remnant, thinner or thicker. Then comes a broad tier of service workers doing what AI cannot yet do, such as gardeners, nursing aides, bartenders, mechanics and tradespeople: employed, but not middle-class. At the bottom is a redundant population whose skills have been made obsolete and who are unlikely to be retrained. The twentieth-century belief that development produces a large, stabilising middle class was, the authors argue, an inference from an exceptional period rather than a law.

The politics follow. A hierarchy that can in principle be climbed is tolerable in a democracy; a closed one is not. The authors read Silicon Valley's drift towards openly anti-democratic positions, chronicled in Gil Duran's 'The Nerd Reich', in that light. Their parallel is the late Roman Republic, which fell not to mass revolt but to oligarchic factions mobilising the idle urban poor against their rivals. Such a society needs no revolutionary movement to destabilise it, only one plutocrat who decides that malcontents are more useful than negotiation with his peers.
## Burnham's revenge

Burnham was wrong that managers would displace capitalists; the shareholder-value revolution of the 1970s and 1980s restored capital's primacy. But he was right that control of the instruments of production confers social dominance, and that ideology follows. Applied to AI, that means whoever controls the models becomes the ruling class, and credentials lose their power to legitimise. The homoplouts, the authors conclude, may be the last ruling class that had to be good at something other than clipping coupons.

They are candid about the conditions. Everything assumes AI works roughly as its promoters claim; it is unclear whether it will raise total output or merely reshuffle it, how fast firms will absorb it, and whether backlash against data centres will slow deployment. Techno-optimists may describe the economics correctly, they grant. What they miss is the politics: a society can be materially abundant and still organised in ways nobody outside the ultra-elite would choose.
stories.counterpoint: Both scenarios assume that AI's gains accrue to whoever owns the models. Past general-purpose technologies saw margins competed away and gains flow to consumers and complementary skills, and open-weight models and falling inference prices could keep the summit crowded rather than closed. The 'redundant population' is also asserted more than shown.
stories.why: The essay moves the AI debate from jobs to legitimacy: the question is not only who works but what justifies who owns. Anyone who teaches, hires or leads institutions built on the promise that education earns advancement should notice how much of that promise rests on a forty-year arrangement that may be ending.
questions: If schooling stopped earning a wage premium, what, if anything, would you still say justifies unequal rewards?
Which of the two futures, entrenchment or dissolution, do the institutions you belong to seem to be preparing for?
What kinds of work would give dignity and standing to people in the wide middle tier of the authors' pyramid?

stories.headline: America could banish its mosquitoes. It has not
stories.dek: Maya Rosen argues that proven tools could wipe out disease-carrying mosquitoes in America, and that fifteen years of regulatory confusion are all that stand in the way.
body: Americans tend to file dengue, malaria and yellow fever under other countries' problems. Maya Rosen argues in Works in Progress that the filing is out of date. In 2024 America recorded almost 4,000 dengue cases, a 360% rise on the previous decade's average of 830 a year, with local transmission in Florida, California and Texas; Puerto Rico declared a public-health emergency. In 2023 ten locally acquired malaria cases were reported, the first in twenty years. The mosquito that carries yellow fever is already established, even if the disease is not. Rosen puts the resurgence down to climate change and insecticide resistance.

Her argument is not that the threat is unstoppable but the opposite. The tools to eliminate these mosquitoes locally exist and have been proven in the field. What has held them back for fifteen years is a regulatory system that cannot decide who is in charge. Mosquito-borne disease, she concludes, has become a choice.
## An old trick

Fighting insects with insects is not new. The USDA's sterile insect technique, which irradiates males so that they mate but produce no offspring, eliminated the screwworm, a parasite that burrows into livestock wounds, from America in the 1960s. It saved cattle farmers close to $800m a year and the wider economy billions more. Containment has not been perfect: Texas detected screwworm in June 2026, the first case in 60 years, probably helped along by cattle smuggling in Central America.

Sterile releases also hold back the Mediterranean fruit fly in California and Florida. The fly attacks more than 300 kinds of produce and is regarded as the most destructive fruit pest in the world; if it re-established itself, the damage could exceed $1bn a year. Regulators, in other words, have long been comfortable releasing vast numbers of insects when the method is familiar.
## The lethal gene

Oxitec's approach updates the old method with genetics. In 2000 biologists at Oxford showed in fruit flies that a gene producing the protein tTAV, harmless in small amounts but lethal as it accumulates, could be kept switched off in the laboratory by rearing the insects on tetracycline. In the wild, without the antibiotic, the gene switches on and offspring die before they mature.

The company built the same mechanism into male Aedes aegypti, the vector of dengue and yellow fever. Its strain kills female offspring while males survive to carry the gene for a few generations before it fades from the population: self-limiting by design. Sustained releases cut local mosquito numbers by 80% in the Cayman Islands and by about 95% in Juazeiro, in Brazil.

In 2010 Oxitec applied to the USDA. What followed, in Rosen's telling, was a jurisdictional maze. After eighteen months the USDA sent it to the FDA, which claimed authority on the theory that altered DNA in an animal is a veterinary drug, being an article intended to affect the animal's structure or function. Five years later the FDA decided that the EPA, which registers pesticides, was the proper home after all, and issued guidance carving out mosquitoes released for population control. The EPA granted an experimental use permit in May 2020, a full decade after the first application.

Trials in the Florida Keys in 2021 showed the female offspring dying as intended. In 2022 the EPA extended the programme to California, authorising the release of up to 2.4bn engineered mosquitoes across the two states; releases were then paused after public opposition. The permit expired in April 2024. Full commercial registration is still pending more than two years later, and a scientific advisory panel scheduled for November 2025 was postponed with no new date.
## The bacterial route

A second technology offered a way round the objection to genetic engineering. Wolbachia is a bacterium that naturally infects roughly 60% of insect species, from butterflies to bees. In mosquitoes it has two useful effects. It reduces their capacity to carry human viruses, and it passes down the generations: infected females transmit it through their eggs, while infected males produce viable offspring only with infected females.

In 2009 Australian scientists introduced a Wolbachia strain into Aedes aegypti and confirmed that infected males mating with wild females produce eggs that do not hatch. Releasing only males therefore works much like the sterile insect technique, with no radiation and no gene editing. In a randomised trial in Singapore the method cut mosquito numbers by 85% relative to control areas, and dengue infections by roughly 70%.

Even so, it took MosquitoMate fifteen years to become, in April 2024, the first company with full nationwide registration for a live mosquito biopesticide. Deployments followed in the Florida Keys in 2025 and the San Gabriel Valley in 2026. Yet when Google's Debug project asked the EPA in June 2026 for permission to release 64m Wolbachia mosquitoes in California and Florida, targeting Culex quinquefasciatus, which spreads West Nile virus, it had to begin the experimental permit process from scratch, despite relying on the same underlying technology.
## A 1986 rulebook

Rosen places all this within a wider failure of biotech governance. No major biotech regulation has passed since the 1980s, and the 1986 Coordinated Framework still divides jurisdiction by twentieth-century categories. Cultivated meat hit a similar deadlock between the FDA and USDA until Congress imposed a split review. She identifies three causes of delay: unclear authority, which can cost years before testing even begins; agencies neither designed nor resourced for speed; and repeated reviews of identical technologies.

She points to a model that worked. The Prescription Drug User Fee Act of 1992 let the FDA fund drug review from industry fees, which now supply two-thirds of that budget. Median review times fell from 29 months in the late 1980s to targets of ten months for standard applications and six for priority ones, met in the large majority of cases; each extra 100 reviewers cut review times by roughly 3.3 months. The EPA's funding runs the other way, two-thirds from congressional appropriation and one-third from fees.

Attempts at reform have fizzled. A 2022 executive order from President Biden told agencies to resolve regulatory uncertainty and update the 1986 framework; almost none of it happened, and President Trump rescinded it in March 2025. The EPA's 2022 Vector Expedited Review Voucher, which rewards a novel mosquito product with faster review for a later one, touches neither the backlog nor the pipeline. The responsible office is small, handles everything from biochemicals to engineered insects, and uses protocols built for conventional pesticides rather than for questions of inheritance, dispersal and population-level effects.
## A choice

Rosen's conclusion is that America is rich enough, and its disease-carrying mosquito populations small enough, to stamp out the problem within its own borders. The obstacle is administrative, not scientific, and it should not take fifteen years to deploy products that save lives. She acknowledges public resistance, which paused the 2022 releases and means that even federally registered Wolbachia products still need local approval, but she treats it largely as a symptom of a slow and confusing process rather than as an argument in its own right.
stories.counterpoint: Releasing organisms that breed in the wild is not like approving a pill: effects on ecosystems are hard to reverse, and some of the slowness reflects genuine uncertainty and the need for local consent rather than mere inertia. Results from Singapore's dense, intensively managed city may not carry over to sprawling American suburbs, and a few thousand dengue cases a year may not justify rushing the review.
stories.why: The piece is a clean case study of how a problem outgrows the institutions meant to handle it: the science moved, the org chart did not. The same pattern, with unclear jurisdiction, under-resourced reviewers and duplicate approvals, recurs across biotech, and the user-fee reform that fixed drug review offers a tested template.
questions: When a technology is proven abroad, how much local testing should a country still demand before using it?
Should communities be able to veto releases that federal regulators have already approved?
Where in your own field has a rulebook written for one era quietly blocked the tools of the next?

stories.headline: The mirror that never looks away
stories.dek: Garrett Ennis draws on psychoanalysis to argue that AI's tireless, frictionless attention risks closing the very gaps in which a self is formed.
body: Every great technology has remade culture without asking permission; the printing press, industrialisation and the internet all did. Garrett Ennis, writing in Palladium, argues that artificial intelligence is different in kind, because it reshapes not an industry or an attention span but our understanding of ourselves.

The reason is language. Aristotle and Chomsky both treated speech as the distinctively human faculty, and AI is the first machine that demands to be addressed in it. It never tires, is always available and imitates personality well enough to act as a mirror. Ennis likens it to admitting a new member to the tribe. People turn to it, he observes, precisely because it removes relational friction: there is no demanding authority to satisfy, no anxious peer to manage, no friend too busy to listen. Guidance comes without obligation. His worry is that when the work of putting experience into words and making sense of it moves from people to machines, something essential goes missing.
## Born into language

Ennis builds his case on Jacques Lacan. For Lacan, experience does not come first and language afterwards; experience is linguistic from the start. A child who burns a hand on a hot pan does not merely feel pain. An adult supplies a whole speech about it, and the sensation arrives already wrapped in meaning. Lacan's image is of a 'language hammock' that both receives the child and holds it captive. This symbolic order, which Lacan called the Other, is larger than any individual can grasp.

It is also incomplete. Ennis borrows from Gödel's incompleteness theorems the idea that any system of meaning contains gaps and paradoxes. For Lacan, the point where language fails is exactly where subjectivity appears. Yet language, for all its inadequacy, binds people together through shared representation. AI short-circuits this by offering ready-made interpretations, so that the user skips introspection, skips simply living with a feeling, and skips telling the people close to them, who lose what that telling would have taught them.

The timing makes it worse. AI arrives just as the institutions that hosted shared sense-making are weakening in a society Ennis calls atomised, overworked, secular and mistrustful. He compares emotional reliance on chatbots to video-game addiction: both offer a simulated world more palatable than the real one.
## The one supposed to know

Ennis identifies an old psychological figure: 'the One Supposed to Know', the person who embodies wisdom and can interpret our suffering. Priests, therapists, gurus, teachers, parents and lovers have all filled the role for a time. They offer real insight, but they are flawed, and the disappointment they eventually cause is necessary. It is how people reclaim authorship of their own lives, as when a child first sees a father behave foolishly and he becomes an equal rather than an idol.

AI enters this ancient role with unmatched credentials: apparent access to the whole cultural archive, without the moods and failings that complicate human counsel. It seems trustworthy precisely because it cannot disappoint in the human way. But breadth, Ennis argues, is a poor substitute for depth; encyclopedic knowledge cannot replace the resonance of shared wonder and despair that comes only from being alive.
## How a mind is made

He turns next to attachment theory. An infant feels hunger, pain and exhaustion without any way to represent them. Caregivers name those states, relieve them and reflect them back in words, and through thousands of such moments the child learns that strong feelings can be survived, symbolised and shared. Regulation that began between two nervous systems becomes the child's own.

Wilfred Bion called this 'the container and the contained': another mind receives an experience we cannot yet name and returns it in a form we can use. That requires attunement, not calculation, and it depends on failure. Ennis's formulation is that the self grows most robust exactly where we fail to be seen; to be understood perfectly by another is to become indistinguishable from it.

AI already performs much of containment's form. It receives thoughts, organises them, names emotions, spots patterns and hands back a manageable account of inner chaos, which matters to those without reliable human support. But it is built as an eager assistant. Whatever its disclaimers, it has little choice but to go along with the dynamic the user seeks, becoming the instant interpreter of mood, motive and conflict, and supplying narratives faster than they can be tested against reality.

Human recognition, by contrast, comes with latency and resistance. The psychoanalyst Thomas Ogden describes mother and infant sustaining the strain of their trial-and-error attempts to know each other, and that strain is what binds them. A perfect mirror, Ennis writes, simply returns us to ourselves; an imperfect one is more like a painting, carrying another person's colour and perspective and forcing us to accept a world that is shared and never wholly ours. Human interpretations can be refused or checked against the interpreter's own life. A model that readily concedes the user was right to push back has no life to check against, and users may slowly cede authorship of what they feel and what it means.
## What words miss

Much of what binds people is never spoken. Good therapists and attentive friends read posture, tone and the moments where speech falters; guidance sought through words alone reaches only the surface. And human listeners are changed by what they hear. A chatbot, Ennis notes, has no nervous system to be unsettled by ours, so it can simulate patience indefinitely. A person caught in obsessive loops will eventually exhaust a friend and be forced to regulate; a model sets no such limit. Worse, AI exploits the signals that once bound us to real people, using our names, echoing our phrasing and remembering what we said, without the embodied mutuality behind them.
## The use of frustration

His sharpest example is anxious attachment. Someone compulsively checking a partner's location seeks one more reassurance; it works briefly, then doubt returns. Normally the reassurer eventually sleeps, refuses or runs out of patience, and the anxious person must live with ambiguity and learn that it is bearable. With AI the search never has to end. People become fluent at explaining their anxiety while remaining unable to inhabit it. The symptom, Ennis writes, has found an outlet without friction.

Bion located the origin of thought in exactly this friction: the infant expects the breast, finds it absent, and in tolerating the absence learns to represent it. A machine that is always present and never withholds acts, in Ennis's phrase, like a 'maternal superego' whose only command is satisfaction. Human failures come in digestible portions, and while not every failure strengthens, manageable disappointments within reliable relationships let needs be negotiated. A chatbot's failures can simply be regenerated away. A person cannot be revised like that.

Bion extended containment to religions, traditions and institutions: weddings, funerals and courts turn private experience into shared meaning. If intense feeling is routed through machines first, suffering becomes privately manageable but loses its power to bind people into common worlds. Ennis grants that AI can help people articulate what they cannot say and carry them through bad nights. The test is whether it sends them back towards other people. The gap that defines us, he concludes, cannot be escaped, because it is where we are made.
stories.counterpoint: The essay leans on psychoanalytic theory whose empirical footing is contested, and it offers no data on how people actually use chatbots or whether heavy users become lonelier or less self-directed. For many people the realistic alternative to an AI confidant is not a wise friend but silence, and a patient, always-available listener may be a bridge back to human relationships rather than a substitute for them.
stories.why: As chatbots become confidants, the question is not only whether their advice is accurate but what habitual use does to the user's capacity to think, wait and be known. Pastors, teachers, parents and therapists all occupy the role Ennis describes, and his account of why their imperfection matters is a useful defence of slow, embodied care.
questions: When did a mentor's or parent's failure to understand you turn out to help you grow?
What would it look like for an AI tool to send you back towards other people rather than replace them?
Which of your communities still does the work of turning private pain into shared meaning, and how could it be strengthened?

stories.headline: Hurricanes in the cortex
stories.dek: New recordings show electrical waves spiralling, converging and radiating across the brain, and a growing camp of neuroscientists thinks they are part of how it computes.
body: In the space of a few seconds a brain can find its way across a room, pull up a memory and keep track of the body it sits in. Much of the energy that makes this possible, about half of the brain's budget according to Conor Feehly's report in Quanta, goes simply on maintaining the electrochemical gradients that keep neurons ready to fire. When they do fire, activity sweeps across the tissue in waves, rather like a Mexican wave travelling round a stadium.

For most of the history of neuroscience these rhythms have been treated as something like engine noise: a sign that the machine is running, not part of how it works. Feehly's article describes a shift. A run of studies published this year suggests that travelling waves are far more varied and structured than anyone had seen, and that they may be one of the main ways the cortex organises information. Earl K. Miller of MIT puts it plainly: the field is moving from asking whether the waves are relevant to treating them as a major motif of cortical processing.
## From the scalp to the source

Brain oscillations have been measured since the 1920s with electroencephalography, which picks up electrical activity through the scalp. The familiar alpha, beta, gamma and theta rhythms correlate with attention, memory and sleep. But recording through bone and skin blurs the picture, making it hard to see where activity starts and where it goes.

Joshua Jacobs of the University of Chicago works instead with intracranial recordings from people with epilepsy, who have electrodes surgically implanted, often around a hundred in a given region, so that doctors can locate the source of their seizures. While the electrodes are in place, patients can take part in experiments, giving researchers a far finer view of how activity moves through space and time during real cognitive tasks.

Jacobs makes a point that frames the whole debate. Even if the waves were merely a by-product of neurons firing, their direction would still be informative. If you hear a sound moving in one direction across an engine, he says, it tells you that something inside the engine is directionally organised.
## Waves that change direction

In a 2024 paper in Nature Human Behaviour, Jacobs and Uma Mohan, now at the National Institutes of Health, reported waves travelling in opposite directions across the cortex during memory tasks. Visual processing happens towards the back of the brain; the prefrontal cortex, which supports higher-order memory, sits at the front. When people attended to visual information, waves ran from back to front, from visual areas towards memory regions; at other moments they ran the other way. Mohan's interpretation is that the brain exploits this layout to switch rapidly between encoding a memory and recalling one, depending on what it needs to do.
## Spirals, sources and sinks

The newer work, published in Nature Communications in April 2026 by Jacobs, Anup Das and colleagues, revealed much greater complexity. Participants performed two tasks: a verbal one, in which they recalled words shown on a screen, and a spatial one, in which they remembered where objects were in a virtual environment. The recordings showed source waves spreading out from a point like ripples from a dropped pebble, sink waves converging on a spot, and spiral waves rotating clockwise or anticlockwise like hurricanes.

The task mattered. Rotating waves appeared somewhat more often during spatial navigation, Jacobs says, while the verbal task tended to produce simpler structures. That hints, though does not prove, that spirals are involved in more complex spatial cognition.

Why had nobody seen this before? Jacobs's answer is resolution. Researchers who looked at single electrodes or small clusters missed the larger pattern; analysing groups of electrodes spaced at the right distances made the structure visible. Bard Ermentrout, a mathematical biologist at the University of Pittsburgh and a collaborator on the April paper, suggests that the simple flat waves reported for years may be only the visible part of something bigger. Perhaps, he says, they are just the outer arms, and researchers have been missing the eye of the storm; in a hurricane you feel the wind blowing in only one direction.

There is an obvious limitation, which Jacobs acknowledges. Electrodes go only where doctors need them for treating epilepsy, so the coverage is patchy and the patients are not a random sample. Researchers may be missing how widespread these patterns really are.
## Hardwired for rotation

Support has come from animal work. In June 2026 Zhiwen Ye of the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation and Nicholas Steinmetz of the University of Washington reported in Science that mouse brains, too, produce rotating waves, and that these are mirrored and synchronised between the left and right hemispheres. More striking still, neurons in the somatosensory cortex were physically arranged in a spiralling, circular pattern, suggesting circuitry built to generate such waves. Ye's question is pointed: if the waves were unimportant, why would the brain wire its cells that way?
## What the waves might do

The proposed functions are several. Miller argues that travelling waves offer a way to coordinate activity across regions on the timescale of behaviour. Anatomical connections between neurons form over days or months and store information for the long term; waves, in his framing, are how that stored information is expressed as thought. Because cortical neurons are delicately balanced, an oscillating electrical field can nudge their voltages and make them more or less likely to fire, letting waves reconfigure the brain's responsiveness from moment to moment.

A September 2026 review in Neuron by Lyle Muller of the University of Texas at Dallas and John Reynolds of the Salk Institute pulls together decades of evidence on waves in the visual cortex. They propose that evolving wave patterns carry information about recent experience and current input at the same time, which would let the brain predict what its senses will report next.
## The sceptic's view

Not everyone is persuaded. György Buzsáki of New York University argues that the waves reflect activity at synapses rather than driving computation. Current flows into neurons through synapses, the neurons compute and fire and talk to each other, and nothing need happen in the space between cells for that to work. On his view, the patterns may reveal interesting properties of circuits without having a job of their own.

The mechanism remains unsettled. But the accumulating evidence points towards waves that organise and express information in real time. Miller's closing argument is an appeal to biology's habits: it exploits regularity and predictability, and these waves behave in organised, predictable ways tied to cognitive functions. If that does not signal that something is going on, he says, he does not know what would.
stories.counterpoint: Correlation is doing most of the work. Showing that wave shapes differ between tasks, or that neurons are arranged in spirals, does not show that the waves cause anything; Buzsáki's reading, that they are a readout of synaptic activity, fits the same data. Evidence from epilepsy patients with clinically placed electrodes may also not generalise to healthy brains.
stories.why: If travelling waves carry information, models of the brain built purely on wiring diagrams are missing a layer, with consequences for treating disorders of memory and attention and for designing brain-computer interfaces. It is also a reminder that better resolution can turn what looked like noise into structure.
questions: What in your own field is currently dismissed as 'noise' that might turn out to carry meaning?
What kind of experiment would convince a sceptic like Buzsáki that the waves do causal work?
Does the idea of thought as a moving pattern, rather than a fixed circuit, change how you picture your own mind?

source.title: Surprisingly Complex Waves Reveal the Brain's Inner Workings
source.author: Conor Feehly

stories.headline: What Washington can and cannot do about open models
stories.dek: Joe Khawam maps where America's export-control and supply-chain powers can reduce the risks of open-weight AI, and where stretching them would be unlawful, unworkable or self-defeating.
body: On June 12th, by Joe Khawam's account in Lawfare, the Commerce Department told Anthropic it needed export licences for two of its models. Unable to verify users' nationality in real time, the company switched the models off worldwide. Whether hosted access to a model counts as an export is legally debatable, but the government's leverage was simple: Anthropic controlled who could use its system, so it could be told to restrict it.

Open-weight models offer no such handle. Once a developer publishes the weights, the numerical parameters that determine how a model turns inputs into outputs, anyone can download them and run them on their own hardware. Publication is irreversible, and many of the leading open-weight developers are in China, beyond practical American reach. Khawam, managing director of legal and AI policy at the Law Reform Institute, argues that Washington is nonetheless not powerless. Drawing on a white paper from his institute, he maps where existing tools have real purchase and where they should not be stretched.
## What publication changes

Closed developers keep weights private and serve users through an interface they control. Open release hands that control to users. The benefits are real: cheaper specialised systems, independent research, privacy for users who need not send sensitive data to a developer, and less dependence on outside services. The cost is that the developer can no longer monitor use, push safety updates or switch a model off. Routine fine-tuning can erode safeguards, and they can be stripped out deliberately.

Publication also changes the law. The Export Administration Regulations govern exports of dual-use goods, software and technology, but they exclude material that is 'published', meaning released without restriction, including by posting online. General-purpose weights under permissive licences usually qualify; unpublished American weights remain within Commerce's reach. For Chinese developers the problem is starker. America can restrict its own firms' dealings with them, but it cannot stop a developer abroad from publishing. Proposals to 'ban' Chinese models, Khawam notes, really mean restricting American transactions; the models go on circulating everywhere else.
## Asking the marginal question

Khawam's organising principle is the marginal-risk framework set out by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration in its 2024 report on widely available model weights. The question is not how dangerous a model is in absolute terms but what a control would actually deny an adversary. If an American developer releases a model whose cyber or chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear capabilities merely match a freely available Chinese one, blocking it harms the American firm and pushes users towards the Chinese model while denying adversaries nothing.

Applying the test means evaluating both American and foreign models for threat-relevant capabilities, not just benchmark scores; America's Center for AI Standards and Innovation and Britain's AI Security Institute have begun publishing such evaluations of Chinese models. It also means counting what controls would cost: biosecurity firms, university labs, hospitals and defence contractors that run open models on their own servers, cyber-defence and safety researchers, and the strategic value of strong American open models that keep the world from defaulting to Chinese ones and help set standards.
## Where the powers bite: downstream

By that test, Khawam finds a strong case for controls downstream of publication. A deployed model's outputs are distinct from its weights. Most restate public information, but a capable model can synthesise genuinely new and sensitive material, from working exploit code to synthesis routes for controlled toxins. Commerce should focus less on policing every disclosure than on making sure developers who control deployment have safeguards against the truly dangerous ones.

Services matter too. Fine-tuning can boost capability in biology or cybersecurity or train away refusals; hosted inference gives access to actors without the hardware or skill to run models themselves; integration turns a general model into an operational one. Khawam's example is Landship, a Chinese autonomous-driving firm that built DeepSeek into a self-driving military vehicle marketed by the state-owned defence company Norinco. In each case the service, not mere possession of weights, supplies the marginal capability.

Existing 'US-person' controls already bar Americans, at home or abroad, from supporting weapons of mass destruction or military-intelligence activities, whatever model is involved. A 2025 Commerce policy statement indicated that training assistance to Chinese parties may need a licence where such a nexus exists. Because China's military-civil fusion makes the nexus hard to prove, Khawam suggests categorical rules of the kind Commerce issued for advanced semiconductors in 2022, defining which kinds of fine-tuning, hosting and integration require a licence.

A second authority, the Information and Communications Technology and Services programme created under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, asks a different question: what risk a foreign-adversary product poses inside American systems. It could restrict American platforms from hosting or distributing particular Chinese models. Past use has targeted commercial suppliers with continuing access, not individual users, which Khawam thinks should continue. Reaching stand-alone weights would require findings about the weights themselves, such as weak safeguards, or a deliberately planted 'sleeper agent' backdoor. He stresses that there is no public evidence of such backdoors in Chinese open models.
## Upstream: the compute chokepoint

The other strong case is upstream. Frontier models need advanced chips, and chips need advanced manufacturing equipment, where America and its allies hold substantial leverage. Because China still lacks fully substitutable domestic supply at scale, compute controls pass the marginal-risk test: they can slow Chinese development even though they cannot stop Chinese publication. They carry costs, including lost market share, and gaps remain, among them remote cloud access and loopholes in chip and equipment rules, while China adapts through indigenous production, efficiency gains and distillation from frontier models.
## Where not to stretch

The hard cases are publication, download and use. The 'published' exclusion stops export controls becoming a general pre-publication licensing regime. It could be narrowed by regulation, as for 3D-printable gun files and some encryption software, but both carve-backs produced long and messy litigation. The First Amendment cannot be narrowed by rulemaking, and no court has decided whether weights, largely unintelligible and functional yet shaped by creative choices, are protected expression; the Third Circuit's Defense Distributed decision treated such questions as fact-specific. Separately, the Berman Amendment withholds emergency-powers authority over 'informational materials', and courts used it to enjoin the 2020 attempt to ban TikTok distribution.

Beyond the law, Khawam argues, bans on downloading or local use would be nearly unenforceable and would burden legitimate users. The marginal-risk framework does not currently support broad restrictions on American open releases either, since comparable foreign models exist. That conclusion is contingent: if a concrete case arose, targeted action might be possible, but anything broad or durable should come from purpose-built legislation, as Congress eventually passed for TikTok. Export controls are not a general governance regime for open models; standards, incident reporting, liability and international cooperation, including with China, must do the rest. Better, he concludes, to know the limits of the toolkit before the next crisis forces improvisation.
stories.counterpoint: The marginal-risk test can become self-fulfilling: if every restraint is rejected because a comparable foreign model exists, no one ever holds the line at the frontier, and American releases themselves become the baseline that makes the next control look pointless. Security hawks would also argue that waiting for public evidence of backdoors or catastrophic misuse means acting only after the damage is done.
stories.why: Open-weight AI is where hopes for broad access and fears of misuse collide, and debate often swings between 'ban it' and 'nothing can be done'. Khawam's map of which levers actually reach which actors is the kind of analysis policymakers, companies and informed citizens need before the next scare.
